claims.text: The proposed surrogate model incorporates experimentally measured, high-resolution microstructural descriptors.
Relevant descriptors include local phase distributions, grain-boundary characteristics, and nanoscale heterogeneities.
The surrogate model will predict Young's modulus more accurately than conventional finite-element simulations.
The surrogate model will predict yield strength more accurately than conventional finite-element simulations.
The surrogate model will predict fracture behavior more accurately than conventional finite-element simulations.
The surrogate model will make predictions more rapidly than conventional finite-element simulations.
Learned correlations between measured microstructural features and mechanical responses enable a multiscale mapping of structure-property relationships.
Using a surrogate mapping bypasses the extensive computation required by detailed finite-element simulations.
The surrogate model is expected to reduce computational time by approximately 50–70% relative to conventional simulations.
The surrogate model is expected to improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15–25% relative to conventional simulations.
The conventional finite-element baseline relies on full-scale computational micromechanical models.
The model may fail when the tested microstructure differs substantially from the microstructures represented in its training data.
Extreme strain rates or temperatures may introduce mechanisms not represented by the surrogate model.
The exact magnitude of the accuracy and computational improvements is uncertain.
The model's robustness across microstructural variations and testing conditions is uncertain.
